text:
Bootstrapped confidence intervals (beginner-friendly)
Resample with replacement to estimate uncertainty without heavy math.

def bootstrap_ci(x, n_boot=2000, ci=0.95, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        sample = rng.choice(x, size=len(x), replace=True)
        means.append(np.mean(sample))
    lo = np.percentile(means, (1-ci)/2*100)
    hi = np.percentile(means, (1+(ci))/2*100)
    return float(np.mean(means)), float(lo), float(hi)

for cond in ['A','B']:
    m, lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(pilot.loc[pilot.condition==cond, 'dwell_time_mean_min'].values)
    print(cond, 'mean≈', round(m,2), 'CI', (round(lo,2), round(hi,2)))

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
What you’ll learn

In plain language A clear mental model of how ML works without math overload — and where it helps (and where it doesn’t) in architectural workflows.


the 12 principles that make ML predictable, not mysterious
how to use generative tools responsibly for studio work
everything reproducible: prompts, seeds, masks, versions


This is the skinned summary. The full detailed deck — pipeline, diffusion, segmentation, surrogate modeling, GH/Honeybee tooling — is the original ML for Architecture PDF.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
How to read each principle
Every principle uses the same four-part frame — the same shape as the course’s own evidence logic:


Idea the principle itself


Why it matters what it changes for you

Quick activity · 2 min apply it to your project

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 1 — ML learns a mapping from examples, not rules
text:
Principle 1 — ML learns a mapping from examples, not rules

Idea An ML model is a function f(x) → y whose parameters are fit from examples (x, y).



Why it matters Expect pattern recognition, not hand-coded logic. The model learns regularities present in the data.


Studio example (massing image) → predicted daylight metric; (facade photo) → style label.



Quick activity · 2 min Name three inputs you could give a model in your current studio project. What output would you want?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 2 — Data is the design brief
text:
Principle 2 — Data is the design brief

Idea The dataset defines what the model can and cannot learn.



Why it matters Better data beats fancier models — curate for coverage and quality, not just quantity.


Studio example A facade-style classifier fails if trained only on one region or era.



Quick activity · 2 min List two gaps in a “facade” dataset that would cause failures on your campus. How would you fill them?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 3 — Representation shapes what can be learned
text:
Principle 3 — Representation shapes what can be learned

Idea How we encode inputs (pixels, meshes, graphs, text) determines what the model can “see”.



Why it matters Choosing a representation is like selecting a drawing type: plan vs section vs perspective.


Studio example Street photos (pixels) for segmentation vs adjacency graphs for layout optimization.



Quick activity · 2 min For your task, would pixels, vectors, meshes, or text be best — and why?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 4 — Loss = what “better” means

Idea The loss function translates “good” into math; models only improve on what loss rewards.



Why it matters If the loss ignores safety or legibility, the model will too. This is your threshold, made explicit.


Studio example A daylight surrogate with MSE learns averages; worst-case glare needs a different objective.



Quick activity · 2 min Write a one-line “loss” for your project (e.g., minimize peak glare while keeping daylight autonomy above target).

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 5 — Training = reduce loss (gradient descent)

Idea Training iteratively adjusts parameters in the direction that reduces loss.



Why it matters Explains learning rate, convergence, and why training looks rough before it stabilizes.


Studio example Don’t judge early iterations; monitor the validation curve, not the first guesses.



Quick activity · 2 min Sketch how you’d know training is “done” (hint: validation loss / early stopping).

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 6 — Generalization is the goal

Idea We care about performance on new, unseen data — not just the training set.



Why it matters Overfitting = memorization; good models transfer to the next site or city.


Studio example A roof-type detector perfect on your curated set fails on cloudy days.



Quick activity · 2 min Name two differences between training images and deployment images. How will you test generalization?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 7 — Bias–variance: too simple vs too specific
text:
Principle 7 — Bias–variance: too simple vs too specific

Idea Underfit models are too simple; overfit models memorize noise.



Why it matters You control this via model capacity, augmentation, and regularization.


Studio example A tiny model misses brick vs terracotta; a huge model memorizes specific buildings.



Quick activity · 2 min Which knob would you turn first to reduce overfit — augmentation, regularization, or more data?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real: treat outputs as suggestions
text:
Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real: treat outputs as suggestions

Idea Predictions are probabilistic; confidence varies by context and input quality.



Why it matters This is the course thesis in ML form: sample multiple outputs and critique; avoid single-image “truth”.


Studio example Use seeds and A/B comparisons for renders, not one lucky frame.



Quick activity · 2 min Generate 3 variations (same seed + small prompt tweaks); choose and justify one.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 9 — Distribution shift breaks models

Idea When deployment data differ from training (climate, culture, camera), expect failure.



Why it matters Plan pilots on real sites; monitor drift; retrain when needed.


Studio example A Berlin-trained segmenter struggles in Bangkok (materials, colors, sky).



Quick activity · 2 min Write one “shift” you expect in your project and a way to detect it.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 10 — Generative models = distributions + conditioning

Idea Diffusion models learn a distribution and sample from it; prompts/masks/refs condition the sampling.



Why it matters Prompts steer; seeds give reproducibility; masks and references preserve geometry and identity.


Studio example Keep geometry via masks; change cladding via prompt; reuse the same seed for versions.



Quick activity · 2 min Take a white-model view; list what you’d mask vs what you’d let the model change.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task
text:
Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task

Idea Pick metrics that reflect the goal and pair them with human A/B judgment for visuals.



Why it matters Numbers alone can reward “pretty wrong” results.


Studio example For concept imagery, use pairwise preference + a rubric (material legibility, camera plausibility).



Quick activity · 2 min Draft two rubric criteria to compare two generated facade images.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 12 — Ethics, IP, and human-in-the-loop

Idea Datasets carry bias; licenses and privacy matter; designers remain accountable.



Why it matters You choose sources, cite them, disclose process, and keep clients safe.


Studio example Use open/owned references; document prompts, seeds, masks; avoid identifying people without consent.



Quick activity · 2 min Pick one slide of your own and add a visible credit line for every image source.

title: A2 Worked Example: External Shading Devices for Offices in Hot Climates
text:
NoteAbout This Example



This is a worked A2 skeleton based on a real research project — “Impact of external shading devices on thermal and daylighting performance of offices in hot climate regions” (Freewan, Solar Energy, 2014). DOI: 10.1016/j.solener.2014.01.009
It starts from a spatial design decision — which shading device to fix to a south-facing office facade — and uses both field measurement and simulation to compare three options. See also the companion data-analysis example for a non-spatial version of the same A2 structure.

title: A2 Worked Example: External Shading Devices for Offices in Hot Climates
text:
1. Decision Recap

Decision
Which fixed external shading device for south-facing offices in a hot-arid climate (Amman, Jordan) best balances cooling-load reduction with maintained task-level daylight?


Alternatives







Option
Description




A — Vertical fins
External vertical aluminium fins projecting from the facade


B — Diagonal fins
External fins mounted at an oblique angle to the facade plane


C — Egg-crate device
Combined horizontal-and-vertical grid (egg-crate geometry) projecting from the facade



All three options were tested on identical south-facing offices at the Jordan University of Science and Technology (JUST) campus. Only the shading device changed; the glazing, room dimensions, orientation, and occupancy were held constant. A fourth condition — the unshaded base case — served as the control.


Audience
Architects and building-services engineers selecting a fixed shading system for south-facing office facades in hot-arid climates, where cooling dominates the energy budget but daylight must remain sufficient for desk work.


Why evidence matters
The instinct choice is often the simplest device — vertical fins are familiar, easy to fabricate, and widely used. But Freewan’s study showed that vertical fins allowed large sun patches to penetrate the office in the afternoon, providing the least cooling relief of the three options (~7% cooling-load reduction vs. base case). The egg-crate device delivered the highest cooling savings (~17%) but cut desk-level illuminance to roughly 200 lux — below the 300 lux task threshold. The ranking of the three options reverses depending on whether you lead with energy or daylight. That tension cannot be resolved by instinct; it requires a controlled comparison.


What action the evidence should support
Select one fixed shading device for the facade, with documented evidence showing the trade-off between cooling-load reduction and maintained daylight for each option.

Workflow definition

Input files: 3D model of the south-facing office; Amman .epw climate file; three shading-device geometry definitions; base case (no shading)
Variable: Shading device type (A / B / C) — the only thing that changes between runs
Steps: Model setup → apply each shading device → run coupled thermal-daylight simulation → extract cooling load, indoor air temperature, and desk illuminance → compare against thresholds → rank
Expected output: Comparison table with cooling-load reduction (%) and illuminance (lux) per option; recommendation stating the trade-off
Threshold: Cooling reduction ≥ 10% vs. base case; illuminance ≥ 300 lux at desk level
Likely failure point: Diagonal fin angle — the oblique geometry makes angular solar transmittance hard to model accurately

title: A2 Worked Example: External Shading Devices for Offices in Hot Climates
text:
5. A4 Branch Declaration

Route
Route A: Retrospective Redesign — this example dissects a published study to show how the A2 structure maps onto a real facade decision. A student using Route B would apply the same comparison structure to their own studio project.


Decision

Project: South-facing office building, JUST campus, Amman, Jordan
Decision: Which fixed external shading device to specify for the south facade
Alternatives: Vertical fins (A), diagonal fins (B), egg-crate device (C)
Why this matters: The device that saves the most cooling energy (egg-crate, ~17%) drops illuminance below the task threshold (~200 lux), while the device that preserves the most daylight (vertical fins, ~350 lux) saves the least energy (~7%). The ranking reverses depending on which metric leads.



Workflow

Primary route: Coupled thermal-daylight simulation (IES-VE, DesignBuilder, or Grasshopper + Honeybee)
Input files: Office geometry, EPW, shading device definitions
What varies: Shading device type (single controlled variable)
Minimum scenarios: 3 shading options + 1 base case (no shading)
Output: Cooling-load reduction (%), indoor air temperature reduction, desk-level illuminance per option
Threshold: Cooling reduction ≥ 10%; illuminance ≥ 300 lux



Feasibility

What must exist by A3: Working simulation model producing cooling load and illuminance for at least Options A and C (the two geometric extremes)
Most likely failure: Angular transmittance of the diagonal fins (Option B) — if the oblique geometry cannot be modeled accurately, compare A vs. C only
Backup route: If coupled simulation is too slow, run daylight-only (Radiance) and use a simplified cooling estimate from shading coefficients
What can be simplified: Report illuminance at one desk position instead of a full spatial grid



Branch Statement

I will use Route A (Retrospective Redesign) to examine how Freewan’s comparison of three fixed shading devices reveals a cooling-vs-daylight trade-off that the design team cannot resolve by instinct, through a controlled comparison of three facade options tested under identical conditions on the same office geometry, because the option that wins on energy loses on daylight and the minimum useful output is a comparison table showing cooling-load reduction and desk-level illuminance for each device against pre-stated thresholds.

title: A2 Worked Example: External Shading Devices for Offices in Hot Climates
section: Why This Example Works as an A2
text:
Why This Example Works as an A2

The decision is spatial and architectural. It starts from a facade, a room, an orientation — not a dataset. The simulation serves the design question.
The ranking is not obvious. Vertical fins preserve the most daylight but deliver the weakest cooling relief. Egg-crate saves the most energy but drops illuminance below the task threshold. Diagonal fins fall between on energy but produce the darkest mornings. No single winner exists — the evidence reveals a trade-off the design team must negotiate.
The controlled variable is clear. Only the shading device changes. Room geometry, glazing, orientation, climate file, and occupancy are held constant across all four conditions (three devices plus base case).
Thresholds are stated before the simulation runs. Cooling reduction ≥ 10%; illuminance ≥ 300 lux. This prevents the post-hoc narrative of “well, 200 lux is close enough.”
The weakest link is named. The diagonal fin’s angular transmittance is flagged as the most fragile input, with a stated backup plan (drop Option B and compare A vs. C only).
The tool choice follows the question. Coupled thermal-daylight simulation is chosen because the question requires both cooling-load and illuminance data on the same geometry — not because it is the most advanced option. A spreadsheet approach is explicitly rejected because it cannot capture how shading geometry interacts with seasonal solar angles.
It is grounded in a real publication. Every number in the comparison table comes from Freewan’s peer-reviewed study. Students can read the full paper to see how the analysis was done and verify the findings independently.







TipAdapting This to Your Studio Project



You do not need a shading study. Replace the three devices with any set of design alternatives you are comparing:

Three site layouts → GIS or Grasshopper, evaluated by walkability, noise exposure, or solar access
Three structural systems → BIM/BEM, evaluated by embodied carbon, span, or construction sequence
Three ventilation strategies → EnergyPlus or CFD, evaluated by air change rate, energy use, or thermal comfort

Keep the structure: one controlled variable, same evaluation method, stated thresholds, named weakest input, and a comparison table where the ranking might change depending on which metric leads. That tension is what makes the evidence useful.








NoteCompanion Example



See also the Hidden Drivers example for a data-analysis version of the same A2 structure, based on Guo et al. (Energy and AI, 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.egyai.2026.100709

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: If you can’t rerun it, it isn’t evidence
text:
If you can’t rerun it, it isn’t evidence
The reproducibility frame
A result becomes evidence only when someone else can inspect how you got it — and ideally reproduce it.

The week’s question If you left the project tomorrow, could someone trust your output without you in the room to explain it?

Documentation is not paperwork after the fact. It is the part of the method that makes the output legible.

Failure
What was lost

AI output treated as final evidence
a claim no one actually checked




The risk is not embarrassment. It is presenting a result you can no longer stand behind.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: When the spreadsheet silently rewrote the data
text:
When the spreadsheet silently rewrote the data
Anecdote · the tool changed your data and didn’t tell you

What happened Geneticists found that Excel was auto-converting gene names into dates and numbers (for example “SEPT2” became a date). A 2016 study found errors in roughly one in five papers with supplementary spreadsheets — the field eventually renamed the genes rather than fight the software.


The lesson Reproducibility starts with knowing what your tool did to your data. Document formats, versions, and import settings — the failure is invisible until someone re-runs it.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
text:
A quick, honest poll
Have you ever struggled to reconstruct what you did on a project from a few months ago?

Almost everyone has. The point is not guilt — it is to treat documentation as a normal, expected part of the workflow, starting with one process today.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Why should you care how an LLM works?
text:
Why should you care how an LLM works?
Model literacy · practical purpose
Understanding the mechanism helps you frame the task, choose the tool and decide what evidence to trust.


Design / studio
Explore deliberately
Generate alternatives around your brief. Specify what may vary and what must stay fixed.


Architectural practice
Delegate an inspectable step
Connect a drawing, script or document to a decision. Keep units, sources and assumptions visible.


Doctoral research
Defend the method
Separate a proposed explanation from evidence. Record the inputs, procedure and checks behind a result.



On each slide: learn the mechanism, then reveal why it matters and what to do differently.


One minute within the existing 15-minute primer. These are overlapping uses, not separate ability levels. Students do not need to design a neural network; they should leave able to make better decisions about their own LLM workflow. Ask them to keep one current architectural or research task in mind. On the next seven slides, show the mechanism first; the first advance reveals its practical consequence and the second reveals a concrete action.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: What happens after you press Send?
text:
What happens after you press Send?
Model literacy · 1 of 7
A common baseline is an autoregressive, decoder-only Transformer: it generates a continuation from the context already available.


01 · Input
Tokens
Text is split into units and represented as vectors.


02 · Context
Causal attention
Layers use the available context, not future answer tokens.


03 · Predict
Next token
The model scores possible next tokens; decoding selects one.


04 · Continue
Append and repeat
Append the token to the context; repeat.



Why it matters: the model generates a continuation conditioned on your input. A worked example and a clear format help define the artifact you want.

Do this: specify “inputs in metres → three overhang options → one comparison table.” Check any performance claim against a source or calculation.



Documented decoder example: Qwen2.5 technical report, §2 (2024).


Allow about two minutes, including the two practice-note reveals. Distinguish the neural-network architecture from architecture as a design discipline. Decoder-only means the text backbone does not need a separate encoder–decoder pair; it does not mean a multimodal product has no image or audio encoders. During training, masked token positions can be processed in parallel. This diagram describes the conceptual generation loop, not every serving optimisation. The model learns conditional patterns and representations, not an arithmetic average of answers. An explicit format makes a draft easier to inspect; it does not guarantee correct content. This mechanism can support complex reasoning, but a fluent facade explanation does not establish that a solar calculation was performed.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: What can attention connect — and what is missing?
text:
What can attention connect — and what is missing?
Model literacy · 2 of 7

Illustrative prompt “Compare 0.6 m and 1.2 m overhangs on this west-facing facade. Explain the likely shading trade-off.”



Available context The model can connect the dimensions, orientation, attached material and earlier messages when forming a response.


Still needs evidence An image may omit scale, location, glazing, weather or occupancy. Attention does not supply missing project measurements or run a simulation by itself.



Why it matters: the project context you supply shapes the comparison. Missing site information may become an unstated assumption.

Do this: attach a labelled plan, north arrow, scale, location and relevant brief. Ask it to distinguish supplied facts, assumptions and missing inputs.



Architectural application of the preceding mechanism, not a model benchmark. A model may infer or recall information, but inferred project inputs must be identified and checked. Distinguish the model’s proposed explanation from a tool result. Avoid teaching that next-token prediction prevents reasoning, or that attention guarantees faithful use of every supplied fact.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: How does a predictor become an assistant?
text:
How does a predictor become an assistant?
Model literacy · 3 of 7


01 · Pre-training
Learn from data
Next-token training develops language, knowledge and patterns useful for many tasks.


02 · Supervised fine-tuning
Learn from examples
Train on demonstrations of useful responses and task behaviour.


03 · Classic RLHF
Learn from preferences
People rank responses → a reward model learns those preferences → reinforcement learning updates the assistant.


RLHF = reinforcement learning from human feedback.

Why it matters: assistant training helps it follow requests and respond usefully. A helpful-sounding endorsement is not an independent design review.

Do this: specify the audience and criteria: client explanation, methods critique or component specification. Ask for the strongest objection, then check its evidence.



One influential recipe, not every model’s training sequence: Ouyang et al., InstructGPT (2022).


About two minutes, including the two practice-note reveals. Training changes model weights; supplying a prompt usually changes the context for that interaction, not the model’s weights. RLHF happens during training, not whenever a person presses a thumbs-up button. Feedback may inform later training, depending on the service. Keep the simplified diagram clearly labelled as the classic recipe. Its reward is a proxy for the qualities being judged, not a certificate of architectural correctness. Do not imply that RLHF inevitably causes agreement or that asking for a critique removes bias.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: A preferred answer and a checked answer differ
text:
A preferred answer and a checked answer differ
Model literacy · 4 of 7








Training signal
What it can reward
Architectural question it leaves open




Human or AI preferences
Useful, clear, appropriate responses
Does this claim hold for this site and brief?


DPO · direct preference optimisation
Preferred responses directly, without classic RLHF’s separate reward-model/RL loop
Do the preferences capture the right criteria?


RL with verifiable rewards
Checkable outcomes, such as correct answers or passing code tests
Are those tests sufficient for the design claim?




Why it matters: passing a test only supports what that test measures. Correct arithmetic for our assumed 3.0 m setback does not establish planning compliance.

Do this: define success first: known cases for code, source fidelity for a literature summary, and explicit comfort/access trade-offs for a design recommendation.



DPO (2023) · Constitutional AI: AI feedback (2022) · DeepSeek-R1: reasoning rewards (2025). The setback is a classroom assumption.


About two minutes. Reward source and optimisation method are different dimensions: DPO may use human or AI preference data. In R1, verifiable math/code rewards are part of a broader training recipe; R1-Zero is the experiment without initial supervised fine-tuning, not a description of every R1 stage. Passing tests provides evidence only for the tested behaviour. Ask what “good” means when energy, access, comfort and design intent conflict.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Stronger systems also do more while answering
text:
Stronger systems also do more while answering
Model literacy · 5 of 7


Reasoning effort A model can spend more computation on intermediate steps before answering. Qwen3 documents adjustable thinking budgets; improvement depends on the task.


Tools and retrieved evidence A system can retrieve a document, execute code or call a tool, then use the result. Those actions add evidence only if the inputs and returned results are checked.




propose a step


execute a tool


inspect its result


revise the decision



Why it matters: more reasoning, more evidence and an executed calculation solve different problems. Extra reasoning time cannot itself supply a missing measurement.

Do this: use reasoning for a difficult comparison, retrieval for a source and code for a calculation. Save the actual sources, inputs and tool outputs.



Qwen3 (2025), §§4.3–4.7 · Anthropic: limits of reported reasoning (2025).


About two minutes. Reasoning effort is inference-time computation, not proof of a new backbone architecture. Retrieval supplies context; it is not retraining. A tool invocation is usually orchestrated by software around the model. Request sources, calculations and a concise rationale, rather than treating a generated reasoning narrative as privileged access to internal computation. Anthropic’s study found omissions in reported reasoning under specific experimental conditions; do not generalise its percentages to every model or architectural task.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Is decoder-only still the whole story?
text:
Is decoder-only still the whole story?
Model literacy · 6 of 7 · evidence checked 4 November 2026








Documented example
What it shows
What to take into practice




Qwen3 · 2025
Dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models; MoE routes each token through selected learned components
More parameters need not mean all are used on every token


Nemotron 3 Ultra · June 2026
A hybrid of Mamba state-space layers and attention, with MoE
Current designs also change how sequences are processed efficiently


Qwen3.5-Omni · April 2026
Text, vision and audio in a multimodal system
A plan or walkthrough can be input; perceived dimensions and performance still need checks




Why it matters: model design changes capability and efficiency, but a bigger parameter count or an “expert” label does not establish skill on your task.

Do this: judge it on a known task from your work: plan reading, document synthesis or tool execution. Record the visible model/mode, result, date and time taken.



Primary reports: Qwen3 · NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra · Qwen3.5-Omni. Examples of mechanisms, not a model ranking.


About two minutes, including the two practice-note reveals. Mamba is a state-space sequence model that maintains and updates a state; hybrids combine it with attention. MoE “experts” are learned network components, not named professionals or necessarily human-readable specialties. Autoregressive generation can survive changes to the internal backbone. Decoder-only remains a useful baseline, not a universal description of every component. These reports document particular public designs; do not infer the undisclosed architecture of a current proprietary service from its output style, latency or benchmark score. One known task is a useful local check, not a general benchmark; log cost if visible, without requiring purchase of a second model.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: What might a more capable design assistant do?
text:
What might a more capable design assistant do?
Model literacy · 7 of 7 · discussion

Plausible direction · not an established capability claim Read a brief and model → propose facade variants → call geometry and simulation tools → compare results against agreed criteria → return a traceable recommendation.



Potentially more automated File preparation, parameter changes, tool execution, error repair and comparison tables.


Still needs a defensible decision Who defines comfort, acceptable trade-offs and missing evidence? Who checks that the simulation represents the intended design?



Why it matters: automation can repeat a workflow faster. If its criteria miss the design question, faster iteration can optimise the wrong thing.

Do this: delegate one repeatable step. State what may change, what stays fixed, how improvement is judged and when the result needs your review.



Use the final two minutes of the literacy block, including the practice-note reveals. This is a teaching speculation grounded in documented tool use and multimodality, not a promise that a product can reliably complete this whole architectural loop. Invite one response: “Which step would you delegate next, and what check would you keep?” Keep model structure, training and runtime orchestration distinct.

text:

Three output types








AI output type
What it is good for
Final-gate check

Final gate AI can help generate an answer. You decide which gate it must pass before it enters the design argument.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Human experience is messy enough that AI can help
text:
Human experience is messy enough that AI can help
Why architecture needs this
Architecture often asks about relationships that are real but hard to reduce cleanly:

spatial atmosphere and perceived calm
thermal acceptability rather than just air temperature
acoustic comfort rather than only decibels
wayfinding confidence rather than only shortest path
facade perception rather than only performance values


A productive use AI can help generate hypotheses for these fuzzy relationships. It cannot validate them. Validation still comes from source checks, simple calculations, field observations, precedent mechanisms, simulations, or sensitivity tests.

Large-Model Method Review
A common situation, examined as a method — not a person.

The artifact A building-performance analysis: polished charts, statistics beyond the author’s stated skill, no understanding of the method when questioned, no disclosure of AI use.


Review it together

which claims are factual, which are relationship-based, and which are workflow/code?
what final-gate checks would have made this trustworthy?
what should have been disclosed, and where?
what is the minimum honest version of this output?


We critique the workflow and its claims, never the author’s ability.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
text:
AI-assisted work, made honest
Key visual
The same four-zone frame as the rest of the course — but now one zone is an AI draft, and the final gate and disclosure are not optional.


Prompt “Draft a setback function: inputs in metres; return pass/fail and the ratio to an assumed 3.0 m threshold.”


AI output a Python function that can become a GhPython component


Final gate 2.4 / 3.0 = 0.8 → fail; 3.0 / 3.0 = 1.0 → pass. Check units and the actual source of the threshold separately.


Disclosure note “AI-assisted arithmetic checked against known cases. The classroom threshold does not establish planning compliance.”



Run the kit A real, runnable example: verified_setback_score.py with its prompt log — AI drafted it, then the output type, known cases, and threshold behavior were checked. See the AI-assisted kit.


Use the function as a bounded example, not a compliance tool. Its internal assertions cover selected ordinary values; they are not exhaustive validation. Save expected and observed outputs, and distinguish the arithmetic check from the separate question of which rule applies. No Python installation is required to discuss the hand-calculable values.


AI can draft the step. It cannot be the final gate for its own output. That gate is your responsibility, every time.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Run one check that could change your mind
text:
Run one check that could change your mind

Lab 23–38 min · individual, with a peer available · one bounded check



Before checking: record the expected result and its basis — a source, known case, manual calculation or observation.
Perform the check: inspect the source, rerun a saved component, calculate a value or compare independent evidence.
Record what happened: expected versus observed result; pass, fail or pending; what the check cannot establish.



Asking the same model “are you sure?” is not an independent check. A second answer can suggest a test; agreement between answers does not validate the claim.


A peer rerun checks whether instructions and saved files reproduce a result; it does not establish physical validity by itself. For a performance claim, distinguish rerunning code from validating assumptions. Do not require students to complete a substantial simulation in 15 minutes: a bounded known case or an honest pending record is acceptable.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
text:
Make the architectural consequence visible

Lab 38–45 min · revise the artifact/claim and complete the existing verification card


Illustrative revision Before: “The AI says this overhang will make the room comfortable.”
After: “The checked shadow geometry supports shade at this time and location. It does not establish thermal comfort. I will retain this option for a temperature, radiation and ventilation comparison.”



Mark the output accept, revise, reject or pending, with a reason.
Save the input, output, check result and revised artifact. Record the visible model/tool name, mode and date; mark unknown details honestly.
Add a dated note to your project page or local draft: peer feedback → check → changed decision → remaining limit.



The sample revision assumes that a shadow-geometry check actually took place. Students must not copy its result without doing an equivalent check. Accepted means adequate for the stated bounded use, not universally valid. Keep the website as a continuation of Week 7’s documentation habit, not a new publishing requirement.

We test documentation the only honest way: someone else follows it cold.

text:
Look harder at what you already did
You learn most by examining the reasoning inside work you have already done — not by adding new work. Every week, the same four questions, pointed at that week’s object:


Did What did I actually do, step by step?


Assumed What did I assume at each step?


Risk Where did I not check — where could it break?


Verify What would I verify if I did it again?


The point is not to judge old work. It is to see how its argument was built.

title: Week 1: Why Evidence Needs a Workflow
text:
Evidence needs a workflow

precedent images can be useful, but rarely prove performance on their own
simulation numbers can be precise, but still depend on assumptions
survey comments can be rich, but need context before they generalize
data only becomes useful when the path from input to decision is legible


A finding is evidence only when someone else can inspect how you got it.

title: Week 1: Why Evidence Needs a Workflow

Sometimes evidence is just vibes


A vibe is not useless It is often the first clue that something might matter.


A vibe is not enough by itself It gets stronger only when the next step asks what would confirm, qualify, or challenge it.


For each image next: name the vibe claim, what it does not show yet, and the next evidence move.

section: When you weight a decision matrix, you are writing a loss function
text:
When you weight a decision matrix, you are writing a loss function

Principle 4 — Loss = what “better” means An ML model only improves on what its loss rewards. Your spreadsheet’s weights are the same thing: they define what “better” means before you compare anything.


So If your weighting ignores a real constraint (cost, daylight, legibility), the “winning” variant will too. Make the criterion explicit, like a loss.

See ML Primer · Principles 3–4.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
section: 2012: a copy-paste error inside a risk model
text:
2012: a copy-paste error inside a risk model

What happened JPMorgan’s “London Whale” risk model lived in a chain of spreadsheets where values were copied and pasted between cells by hand. One step divided by a sum instead of an average, understating the risk. The losses reached about US$6 billion.


The lesson A spreadsheet is a transparent comparison layer only if its steps are inspectable. Manual copy-paste between cells is exactly where the logic stops being traceable.

text:
A prototype makes one workflow step inspectable
A workflow is the sequence that turns inputs into an output. A prototype is a small working version you can run and inspect.


Input The file, geometry, data, or values you start with.


Change The one variable you alter. State what stays fixed.


Output The value, table, figure, or geometry you save.


Check A specific comparison that can reveal an error.



Make these four labels explicit in your test, walkthrough, and project page.

The missing record

Traceability lets another person inspect how an output was produced.


Retains the original reproducibility examples: the departing analyst, a spreadsheet that works on one machine, undocumented GIS clipping, and a notebook that depends on a silently edited file. Use these as examples of missing records, not judgments about student competence.

Most fair questions fall into three families. Draft one honest answer for each.


Method “How do you know the sample / model is adequate?” → state your check and its limit.


Implementation “What would this cost or take to apply?” → give a range, not a guess.


Alternatives “Could something else explain this?” → name the alternative you ruled out, and how.



A question is a chance to show your reasoning, not an attack to defend against. Acknowledging a limit builds more credibility than deflecting.

Why Run EnergyPlus Outside GH First?
This is not an argument against Grasshopper, Ladybug, or Honeybee. Those tools are useful design interfaces, and the output can still be patched back into GH later.
The direct CLI run is a visibility exercise. It lets students inspect the model file, weather file, run period, thermostat setpoints, output variables, warnings, and CSV outputs before adding another translation layer. That reduces uncertainty while students learn what the simulator actually did.

extracts monitored hourly outputs and thermostat setpoints to a clean CSV

The point is not to prove a design. The point is to show what must be inspected before a simulation result becomes evidence.

NoteAbout This Example



This is a worked A2 skeleton based on a real research project — “Toward smarter HVAC control: Machine learning reveals hidden drivers in thermal comfort databases” (Guo et al., Energy and AI, 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.egyai.2026.100709

title: A2 Worked Example: Hidden Drivers in Thermal Comfort Databases
text:
1. Decision Recap

Decision
Which representation of missing radiant-temperature data should be used when training thermal comfort models from field-study databases?


Alternatives








Label
Treatment
Description




T1
Rule-based imputation
Replace missing mean radiant temperature (\(T_{mrt}\)) with air temperature (\(T_a\)), following standard practice


T2
Learning through missingness
Let the model learn from the pattern of what is missing, using missingness indicators as input features


T3
Measured-only subset
Drop all records without measured \(T_{mrt}\) and train only on complete cases





Audience
Researchers and standards committees who rely on thermal-comfort databases (ASHRAE Global Thermal Comfort Database II, etc.) to calibrate models used in HVAC sizing and control.


Why evidence matters
The default assumption — impute \(T_{mrt} = T_a\) — enters every downstream model silently. If this treatment distorts the learned relationship between air and radiant conditions, then every comfort prediction and every control policy built on it inherits that distortion. The question is whether the conclusion survives a reasonable change in how missing data is handled.


What action the evidence should support
Decide whether the standard imputation practice should be replaced, supplemented with sensitivity reporting, or flagged as a known limitation in future database-driven comfort studies.

Decision

Decision: Whether the standard missing-data treatment (\(T_{mrt} = T_a\)) produces a stable or unstable learned sensitivity
Alternatives: Three data treatments (T1, T2, T3)
Why this matters: Every HVAC control strategy and comfort standard that relies on these databases inherits the data treatment silently

Input files: Database CSV + metadata audit
What varies: Data treatment (the single controlled variable)

What can be simplified: Drop T3 (measured-only) if the subset is too small to train on



Branch Statement

I will use Route A (Retrospective Redesign) to test whether the learned air-to-radiant sensitivity in thermal comfort models is stable across data treatments, through a controlled comparison of three imputation strategies on the same database, because the design decision (which treatment to trust) depends on whether the conclusion survives the space of reasonable data-cleaning choices, and the minimum useful output is the sensitivity ratio under each treatment with the learning model and validation splits held fixed.

title: A2 Worked Example: Hidden Drivers in Thermal Comfort Databases
section: Why This Example Works as an A2
text:
Why This Example Works as an A2
This example demonstrates several things the assignment is looking for:

The decision is about evidence, not about software. The question is not “which tool should I use” but “does the conclusion change when I handle the evidence differently.”
The alternatives are genuine. All three treatments are defensible. The point is to test whether the choice matters, not to declare one correct.
The workflow has a controlled variable. Only the data treatment changes; the model, validation splits, and target are held fixed. This is what makes the comparison interpretable.
The threshold is stated in advance. “If the ratio changes by more than 50%” is a pre-committed criterion, not a post-hoc narrative.
The failure modes are named. Record misclassification is acknowledged as the weakest link, not hidden.
The tool choice follows the question. Python/notebook is chosen because the question requires retraining a model under controlled conditions — not because Python is the most advanced option.







TipAdapting This to Your Own A2



Replace the database with your evidence source. Replace the three data treatments with three versions of your studio decision (three site layouts, three facade options, three scoring methods). Keep the structure: one controlled variable, same evaluation method, stated threshold, named failure mode.

Regression: predict cooling energy from design inputs
We fit a simple linear model and evaluate on a held-out test set.

features = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation','glazing_u_w_m2k']
target = 'cooling_kwh_m2'
X = df[features]
y = df[target]

cat = ['orientation']
num = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','glazing_u_w_m2k']
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), cat),
    ("num", 'passthrough', num)
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
reg = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('model', LinearRegression())])
reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = reg.predict(X_test)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, pred)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred)
r2, mae


plt.scatter(y_test, pred, alpha=0.8)
plt.xlabel('Actual cooling kWh/m²')
plt.ylabel('Predicted')
plt.title(f'Linear Regression: R²={r2:.2f}, MAE={mae:.1f}')
m = np.array([y_test.min(), y_test.max()])
plt.plot(m, m, 'k--', alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

text:
Classification: comfortable daylight?
Define a simple label: comfortable if glare_probability < 0.35 and daylit_area > 0.5.

df['comfortable'] = ((df['glare_probability'] < 0.35) & (df['daylit_area'] > 0.5)).astype(int)
Xc = df[['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation']]
yc = df['comfortable']
pre_c = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), ['orientation']),
    ("num", 'passthrough', ['wwr','shading_depth_m'])
])
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=yc)
clf = Pipeline([('pre', pre_c), ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
clf.fit(Xtr, ytr)
predc = clf.predict(Xte)
acc = accuracy_score(yte, predc)
cm = confusion_matrix(yte, predc)
acc, cm


confusion_matrix_plot(cm, class_names=("Not Comfortable","Comfortable"), title=f'Logistic Regression (Accuracy={acc:.2f})');

We vary model complexity (polynomial degree) and show CV scores.

deg_scores = []
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for deg in range(1,7):
    poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=deg, include_bias=False)
    pipe = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('poly', poly), ('ridge', Ridge(alpha=1.0))])
    scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
    deg_scores.append((deg, scores.mean(), scores.std()))

ds = pd.DataFrame(deg_scores, columns=['degree','cv_mean','cv_std'])

Key ideas

Always hold out test data or use cross-validation
Start simple; only add complexity if it improves validated performance
Document random seeds and settings for reproducibility
“Deep” models need more data and care; don’t overfit
